title: Shloka 115
subtitle: Needing nothing, reached by goodwill, watching the end

namas.translation: Since she lacks nothing, no satisfaction of hers depends on anything being supplied.
For those attached to her she is the hoard itself, the wealth kept in reserve against every need.

morphology.note: nidhi is lexically masculine; here it stands as a feminine epithet of the goddess.

compound.gloss: she who is the treasure of her devotees

namas.translation: She holds the reins, restraining and directing as a charioteer does an unruly team.
Nothing whatever falls outside her rule, since the word nikhila leaves no remainder.

compound.gloss: she who is sovereign over everything

namas.gloss: Attained Through Friendliness And Its Kin
namas.translation: The settled dispositions of goodwill, compassion, gladness and evenness make the mind fit to receive her.

compound.gloss: she who is reached through the dispositions beginning with friendliness

children.gloss: a settled impression in the mind, an abiding disposition

namas.translation: When the worlds are reabsorbed at the close of an age she alone remains, looking on at their disappearance.

compound.gloss: she who is the witness of the universal dissolution

children.gloss: reabsorption, the destruction of the world
she who observes as an eye-witness

commentary.meaning: Four of the six names in the first line begin with the syllable ni, and the repetition is doing more than decorating the line: nitya, nidhi, niyantrī, nikhila carry the verse from what she is in herself to what she is for someone else and then to what she is over everything. She is permanently satisfied, which is to say that her fullness is not the result of anything having been supplied to her. She is nevertheless a hoard for those attached to her, and this is the first thing the verse says about a relation. She holds the reins; she rules with nothing left outside. The second line changes both the sound and the subject, turning to m and asking two different questions: how she is reached, and what she is doing when everything else has stopped. The two halves answer each other. Someone who needs nothing cannot be bought, so the verse specifies the only currency that works — the settled dispositions of goodwill, compassion, gladness and evenness — and then sets her at the one moment when there would be nothing left to offer her in any case, looking on while the worlds go out.
commentary.history:
Nityatṛptā is built on √tṛp, to be satisfied, the root behind tṛpti and behind the tarpaṇa offerings of water by which the ancestors are refreshed. That background gives the name its edge. Much of Indian ritual assumes an economy in which the gods are fed and, being fed, give; against it the hymn says that this deity is satisfied nityam, with no supplier and no interruption, so that nothing offered to her improves her condition. The Bhagavad Gītā says the same of the liberated person in its third chapter, calling him ātmatṛpta, satisfied in the self, and concluding that no action remains for him to do. Applied to the goddess, the term takes the transaction out of worship without taking away worship, a difficulty the tradition leaves standing.

The next name supplies the other half of that difficulty. A nidhi is a hoard in the plain material sense: treasure buried in the ground, a deposit laid up against future need, of the kind Kubera is said to keep. Bhaktanidhiḥ is a genitive tatpuruṣa, and Sanskrit leaves the direction of a genitive undetermined: the treasure belonging to her devotees, which is the usual reading, or, with more strain, a treasury whose contents are devotees. What is unusual here is grammatical. Nidhi is masculine, and the hymn presses it into service as a feminine epithet without altering the stem; the recitation lists preserve this by giving the dative as bhaktanidhaye rather than the -yai expected elsewhere. The seam has not been sanded down.

Niyantrī comes from ni-√yam, to hold in, restrain, control. The unprefixed agent noun yantṛ means a driver or charioteer, one who holds reins; the same root with the instrument suffix gives yantra, a device that holds something in place. The chariot is not an accident of vocabulary: the Kaṭha Upaniṣad's celebrated image makes the body a chariot, the intellect its driver, the mind the reins and the senses the horses. The Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad supplies the theological version in its dialogue on the antaryāmin, the inner controller who dwells in earth, sun, mind and self alike, controls them from within, and is unknown to them. Niyantrī is the feminine of that office, and it sits between the treasury and the sovereignty: she is not only generous, she is also holding the reins.

Nikhileśvarī turns on a word worth taking apart. Khila in older usage means a gap, a piece of fallow ground, and by extension a supplement appended to a finished text. A-khila therefore means without gaps, entire; ni-khila is formed the same way. The word does not say large, it says without remainder, and placed immediately after niyantrī it extends the reins over the whole field rather than the well-behaved part of it.

The fifth name is the surprising one. Maitryādivāsanālabhyā points unmistakably at the thirty-third aphorism of the first chapter of Patañjali's Yoga Sūtra, which prescribes friendliness towards the happy, compassion towards the suffering, gladness towards the meritorious and indifference towards the wicked, and says the mind is thereby made clear. Those four attitudes, under the same names, are the four immeasurables of Buddhist meditation, and their presence in both traditions shows how much vocabulary the meditative schools of India held in common. The name changes one word: Patañjali says bhāvanā, deliberate cultivation, while the hymn says vāsanā, the settled residue that long habit leaves behind — which raises the requirement, since a vāsanā is what remains when the practice has stopped being a practice. And labhyā is strong — obtainable, to be got — not merely pleased or propitiated. A hymn otherwise occupied with diagrams and syllables here makes decency towards other people the condition of access.

Mahāpralayasākṣiṇī closes the verse at the end of time. Purāṇic cosmology distinguishes several orders of dissolution, and the mahāpralaya is the one at the end of Brahmā's own lifespan, when the elements collapse into their causes and, in the Sāṃkhya account the Purāṇas borrow, the whole hierarchy of evolved principles is withdrawn into unmanifest nature in the reverse of the order by which it emerged. Sākṣin is an old compound of sa and akṣi, with the eye: one who saw the thing himself, hence a legal witness, and in Vedānta the name for consciousness insofar as it observes without being implicated. The Devī Māhātmya opens on this scene: the ocean of dissolution, the sleeping Viṣṇu, and the goddess as the sleep itself. To call her witness of the great dissolution is to say that when there is nothing left to be conscious of, there is still someone conscious.
commentary.practice:
This is one of the easier verses in the hymn to recite and one of the easier ones to lose your place in, for the same reason: the first line gives you four names beginning with ni and almost nothing else to hold on to. Nitya, then the nidhi buried in the middle of the second name, then niyantrī, then nikhila. Fix the order by its sense rather than its sound — satisfied, treasury, restrainer, ruler — and the line stops sliding.

The second and third names are joined by a sandhi that the written form makes obvious and the spoken form can obscure. Bhaktanidhiḥ ends in visarga; before the voiced n of niyantrī the visarga becomes r, and the printed text accordingly reads bhaktanidhir niyantrī, run together without a break. Do not restore the ḥ because you know the dictionary form. Say the r lightly, as a single tap, and go straight on.

Niyantrī contains the cluster ntrī: dental n closed at the teeth, dental t released, then r, then the long ī. English has no sequence like it and will want to lose the t in the middle. Practise it at half speed. Maitryādi has the reverse problem, three consonants after the diphthong — t, r, y — and the diphthong is a full long vowel, mai, not the short glide of the English word my. In mahāpralayasākṣiṇī the conjunct kṣ is a single articulation, guttural k followed immediately by retroflex ṣ, and the ṇ after it is retroflex because of it: Sanskrit converts a dental n to ṇ after certain preceding sounds, which is why the word is sākṣiṇī and not sākṣinī. That rule operates all through the hymn, in rūpiṇī and its relatives.

Metrically the verse is a clean anuṣṭubh, four quarters of eight syllables, with the break after nikhileśvarī. Both names in the second line fill an entire half-line by themselves, so the pace has to slow there whether or not you intend it to. That is the natural place to breathe.

For the recitation performed as archanā, with a flower or a grain of rice set down at each name, the six become nityatṛptāyai, bhaktanidhaye, niyantryai, nikhileśvaryai, maitryādivāsanālabhyāyai and mahāpralayasākṣiṇyai. Note two things. The ī-stems contract before the ending, so niyantrī gives niyantryai and not niyantrīyai, and the same happens to nikhileśvarī and sākṣiṇī. And bhaktanidhaye breaks the pattern entirely, because the underlying noun is a masculine i-stem; this is the one name in the verse that will sound wrong to an ear trained on the rest of the thousand, and it is supposed to.

As for what the verse asks of the reciter: the fifth name is a plain statement that a particular kind of interior weather is the price of admission, and that no amount of technical accuracy substitutes for it. Friendliness towards those doing well, compassion towards those who are not, gladness at other people's good conduct and evenness towards those behaving badly are not advice appended to the practice. They are named as the means by which she is obtained, and they are tested outside the recitation rather than in it.

crossReferences.deva: द्वा सुपर्णा सयुजा सखाया समानं वृक्षं परिषस्वजाते । तयोरन्यः पिप्पलं स्वाद्वत्त्यनश्नन्नन्यो अभिचाकशीति ॥
crossReferences.iast: dvā suparṇā sayujā sakhāyā samānaṃ vṛkṣaṃ pariṣasvajāte | tayor anyaḥ pippalaṃ svādv atty anaśnann anyo abhicākaśīti ||
crossReferences.translation: Two birds, companions always together, cling to the same tree. One of them eats the sweet fruit; the other does not eat, and looks on.
crossReferences.relevance: The oldest image in the tradition of the two names that frame this verse. The bird that does not eat is nityatṛptā, satisfied without being fed; the bird that looks on is the sākṣin, the witness, and the verb abhicākaśīti is an intensive form — it does nothing but look, and looks hard. The hymn separates the two ideas by four names and a change of metre, but they are the same bird.

crossReferences.deva: आत्मानं रथिनं विद्धि शरीरं रथमेव तु । बुद्धिं तु सारथिं विद्धि मनः प्रग्रहमेव च ॥
crossReferences.iast: ātmānaṃ rathinaṃ viddhi śarīraṃ ratham eva tu | buddhiṃ tu sārathiṃ viddhi manaḥ pragraham eva ca ||
crossReferences.translation: Know the self as the rider in the chariot and the body as the chariot itself; know the intellect as the driver and the mind as the reins.
crossReferences.relevance: Niyantrī is the feminine agent noun from ni-√yam, to hold in, and the unprefixed form of the same noun is the ordinary word for a charioteer. This is where that vocabulary lives in the older literature. The verse also supplies the reason the name is not merely a synonym for ruler: a driver restrains in order to arrive somewhere.

crossReferences.translation: Clarity of mind comes from cultivating friendliness, compassion, gladness and indifference, directed respectively towards the happy, the suffering, the meritorious and the unmeritorious.
crossReferences.relevance: The source of the phrase maitryādi and the reason the name can leave the remaining three attitudes unspoken: any reader with training would supply them. Patañjali's word is bhāvanā, deliberate cultivation; the hymn substitutes vāsanā, the disposition that cultivation eventually leaves behind, and thereby raises the requirement.

references.title: Lalitā Sahasranāma with Bhāskararāya's Commentary
references.author: tr. R. Ananthakrishna Sastry (Adyar Library and Research Centre; frequently reprinted)
references.note: The standard route into the Saubhāgyabhāskara for readers without Sanskrit. The English is Victorian and the translator abridges, so treat it as a guide to what the commentary is doing rather than as the commentary itself. What it shows well is how much of the traditional exegesis consists of grammatical derivation — the commentator's first move on a name like niyantrī is almost always to name the root.

references.title: The Early Upaniṣads: Annotated Text and Translation
references.author: Patrick Olivelle (Oxford University Press, 1998)
references.note: Sanskrit and English on facing pages, with notes that tell you where the text is uncertain instead of smoothing it over. For this verse, read Kaṭha 1.3 for the chariot behind niyantrī and Bṛhadāraṇyaka 3.7, the dialogue on the inner controller, which is the doctrinal ancestor of the name.

references.title: The Yoga Sūtras of Patañjali: A New Edition, Translation, and Commentary
references.author: Edwin F. Bryant (North Point Press, 2009)
references.note: Worth the bulk. Bryant gives each sūtra with Vyāsa's commentary and the later subcommentators, so on 1.33 you can watch the tradition argue about whether the four attitudes are ethics or technique. The answer bears directly on why a tantric hymn would make them a means of access.

references.title: Classical Hindu Mythology: A Reader in the Sanskrit Purāṇas
references.author: Cornelia Dimmitt and J. A. B. van Buitenen (Temple University Press, 1978)
references.note: Translated extracts arranged by theme, including the cosmological sections on the ages of the world and the orders of dissolution. Read the material on pralaya before deciding what mahāpralayasākṣiṇī is a witness to; the Purāṇas are more specific about the mechanics than most summaries suggest.

references.title: A Sanskrit-English Dictionary
references.author: Monier Monier-Williams (Oxford, 1899)
references.note: Four entries repay a look here: khila, which turns out to mean a gap or a patch of waste ground and explains why nikhila means entire; nidhi, with its buried-treasure senses; vāsanā, where the range from perfume to mental residue is set out; and sākṣin, where the derivation from sa plus akṣi is given.
